title: What convexity buys, and what it doesn't
sub: Convexity guarantees the destination; conditioning decides the speed.

frames.caption: Gradient descent on f = (L x² + μ y²)/2, a convex bowl. Here L = μ = 1, so the level sets (grey) are circles, the gradient points straight at the minimum, and a good step lands on it almost immediately.
Stretch the bowl: L = 10, μ = 1, condition number κ = L/μ = 10. The gradient now points mostly across the narrow valley, not along it. Steps bounce from wall to wall while creeping along the floor.

κ = 50: still convex, still a unique minimum, still guaranteed to converge, but each step makes only a sliver of progress along the long axis. The number of steps grows in proportion to κ. This is why conditioning, not just convexity, decides how fast optimization is, and why preconditioners, Adam-style scaling and second-order methods exist.
Now a non-convex function, g(x) = x⁴ − x² + 0.1x, from the post. Two gradient descent runs start close together, at x = −0.2 and x = 0.3.
Each follows its own local slope downhill. They head into different valleys.

Both converge, to different points. The left one finds the global minimum (g ≈ -0.322); the right one is stuck in a local minimum (g ≈ -0.181) and, with plain gradient descent, can never leave: every nearby point is worse. In a convex function this cannot happen, because any local minimum is the global one.
